text:
A free online book: LLM Inference Handbook by Sherlock Xu (2026).

This book is a practical technical reference for engineers deploying, scaling, and operating language models in production.

It brings together the concepts and decisions involved in turning a trained model into a responsive, cost-aware service, from model behavior and hardware selection to application interfaces and ongoing operations.

Readers can use it as a guided progression or as a lookup resource for specific engineering questions.

Read the book online on @ChapterPal: https://www.chapterpal.com/book/3fef12a8-4dcd-412e-bd1f-5105591d515c/llm-inference-handbook
title: ChapterPal — AI-assisted reading and note-taking

text:
For decades, the idea of AI improving itself was just a thought experiment. Today, AI is already helping researchers at frontier labs run experiments, write code and test ideas faster. So how far are we from AI that can do the research on its own?

In our first episode of Working Theory, a16z General Partner Sarah Wang explores recursive self-improvement with two leading AI researchers: Mark Chen, Chief Research Officer at OpenAI, and John Schulman, co-founder and Chief Scientist of Thinking Machines Lab, and co-founder of OpenAI.

They cover what RSI actually means, why research taste is so hard to teach, and why AI may be one of our best tools for solving alignment.

00:00 The last invention
01:58 What is RSI?
03:21 How far are we?
05:56 Getting to full RSI
10:57 Aligning RSI
15:08 Working theory

YouTube: http://youtu.be/h_aA1-R70E8

🔌 USB plug-in to a calibrated, moving robot arm in ~10 mins
🌐 MuJoCo right in the workspace (adjust physics & scenes via chat!)
